Wealthtender (published August 13, 2025) describes fee transparency as a competitive advantage with a 73% priority, noting clear fee communication is a powerful differentiator.
Nearly half of survey participants (48%) said pricing and overall anticipated costs are among the top three factors that lead them to choose one advisor over others (published August 13, 2025).

Merrill Lynch disclosed new data analytics and shelf fees in updates to its Form ADV, stating it will have a financial incentive to recommend products from third-party firms that pay those fees (trade report published September 29, 2026).

A survey of people hiring financial advisors (published August 13, 2025) found that just over 38% of people consider a lack of transparency about fees or commissions a major red flag, and that if an advisor cannot clearly explain their pricing structure it undermines trust.

Schwab's CEO stated on the 2025 second-quarter earnings call (quarter ended June 30, 2025) that for 50 years Schwab has innovated from a standpoint of what is right for clients, alongside regulators, in a way that creates transparency, low-cost, effective markets.

Morgan Stanley states in its 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) that its broker-dealers are subject to the SEC's Regulation Best Interest, which requires them to act in the best interest of retail customers when making a recommendation without placing their own interests ahead of the customer's. Why it might matter: Morgan Stanley notes its investment advisory client relationships are also subject to fiduciary obligations and that the SEC and other supervisory bodies have broad administrative powers to address non-compliance.

Edward Jones states in its 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) that it is subject to the SEC rule requiring delivery of a Form CRS Relationship Summary informing clients of fees, costs, conflicts of interest, and disciplinary history. Why it might matter: Edward Jones notes the SEC has also issued guidance clarifying the fiduciary standard applicable to advisory relationships.

Raymond James states in its 2025 10-K (period ended September 30, 2025) that Regulation Best Interest and Form CRS required it to implement additional client disclosures and education, and that various states have proposed or adopted differing conduct standards. Why it might matter: various states have also proposed or adopted laws and regulations seeking to impose new standards of conduct on broker-dealers.

Raymond James states in its 2025 10-K (period ended September 30, 2025) that the UK FCA Consumer Duty, effective July 31, 2023, requires firms to deliver good outcomes for retail customers with respect to price and value, among other things. Why it might matter: in April 2024 the Department of Labor issued a final rule significantly expanding the definition of investment advice fiduciary under ERISA.

Morgan Stanley states (Form ADV, published November 4, 2026) that under DOL regulations under ERISA Section 408(b)(2), it must provide information on its services and compensation to fiduciaries to assess the reasonableness of compensation. Why it might matter: Bank of America separately notes increasing pressure to provide products and services on more attractive terms, including lower fees, lower cost investment strategies and higher interest rates on deposits.

Merrill Lynch states (Form ADV, published October 30, 2026) that under DOL regulations under ERISA Section 408(b)(2), it must provide compensation information to fiduciaries and plan sponsors of retirement accounts to assess the reasonableness of compensation. Why it might matter: the firm states this information is provided at the outset of the relationship through Retirement Account Addendum/408(b)(2) fee disclosures.

Raymond James states (10-Q, period ended June 30, 2026) that beginning August 2024 the SEC's Division of Enforcement requested information regarding its cash sweep program practices for advisory clients and has reportedly conducted similar reviews at other institutions. Why it might matter: the firm states it has been cooperating with this inquiry.

Schwab states (Form ADV, published October 15, 2026) that the SEC found it made false and misleading statements in Form ADV Part 2A brochures about cash allocations in Schwab Intelligent Portfolios accounts, including its conflict of interest in setting cash allocations. Why it might matter: Schwab states the SEC found the firm and its former affiliate violated provisions of the Advisers Act from March 2015 through November 2018.

Merrill Lynch states (Form ADV, published October 30, 2026) the SEC issued an administrative order finding its wrap fee program disclosures contained a material misstatement because a production credit fee was charged but not disclosed alongside the disclosed currency mark-up. Why it might matter: the SEC order also found a failure to adopt and implement written policies and procedures reasonably designed to address the relevant fee disclosure.

Schwab states in its 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) that regulations governing broker-dealers cover, among other things, fee arrangements, order flow revenue, disclosure to clients, and fiduciary duties. Why it might matter: Schwab states the principal purpose of regulating these entities is the protection of clients and securities markets.

A trade report (published November 4, 2026) states that under the SEC's Marketing Rule (Rule 206(4)-1), financial firms are legally exposed if they promote third-party ratings or badges that cannot be verified as completely impartial. Why it might matter: the report states such awards posed a reputational risk for Morgan Stanley and potentially multi-million dollar SEC penalties.

Schwab states in its 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) that the SEC withdrew the proposed Order Competition Rule and Regulation Best Execution in June 2025, which the company had been evaluating. Why it might matter: Schwab also states the FDIC withdrew certain notices of proposed rulemaking on March 3, 2025.

Industry commentary (trade report published September 30, 2026) notes the SEC is sustaining its focus on cash sweep disclosures, and a wave of litigation against major firms over allegedly low client yields keeps the question of who benefits from rising rates on uninvested cash alive in client conversations. Why it might matter: the report states advisors should be prepared to explain how their custodian's sweep structure works and how it may shift with the rate environment.

State securities regulators led by NASAA announced a combined $4.4 million settlement with Wells Fargo and Merrill Lynch over charges of unreasonable commissions on small-dollar retail equity transactions, with restitution ordered on over 256,000 transactions over a five-year period (trade report published October 16, 2026). Why it might matter: the investigation was led by Massachusetts and joined by regulators in multiple other states.

A Wealthtender publication (published August 13, 2025) states the SEC established a rule in 2021 requiring advisors who display only a handful of self-picked testimonials on their website to also link to an online location where all of their reviews can be read. Why it might matter: the source advises that testimonials on an advisor's website are useful only if accompanied by a link to a location where all reviews can be read.

Schwab's 2025 second-quarter earnings call (quarter ended June 30, 2025) references the mid-May reduction of the SEC 31 fee rate. Why it might matter: Schwab separately noted a slight offset in its other revenue line due to the SEC's decision to lower exchange processing fees to zero beginning in mid-May, a rate change it described as P&L neutral.

Schwab's President and CEO stated on the 2025 second-quarter earnings call (quarter ended June 30, 2025) that the firm wants to work alongside regulators in a way that creates transparency, low-cost, effective markets. Why it might matter: the CEO said any new innovation should expand on the transparency and low-cost markets Schwab already enjoys, not move backwards.

The SEC entered a settlement order with Morgan Stanley Wealth Management finding that from 2009 through 2015 it inadvertently charged advisory fees in excess of what had been disclosed to and agreed to by its legacy clients (Form ADV, published November 4, 2026). Why it might matter: the settlement also found that from 2002 to 2016 the firm's predecessors charged fees in excess of what was disclosed to and agreed to by their clients.

Morgan Stanley states in its 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) that it has experienced pricing pressures as competitors seek to obtain market share by reducing prices and fees, paying higher interest rates on deposits, eliminating commissions or other fees, or otherwise providing more favorable terms of business. Why it might matter: the firm states certain competitors may be subject to less stringent legal and regulatory regimes, putting it at a competitive disadvantage.

Raymond James states in its 2025 10-K (period ended September 30, 2025) that regulatory requirements have resulted in greater price transparency, leading to price competition and decreased trading margins, and that trading margins have been further compressed by the shift from high- to low-touch services, while some competitors seek to obtain market share by reducing fees, commissions, or margins. Why it might matter: the firm states it periodically may need to adjust its fees, commissions, margins, or interest rates on deposits to remain competitive.

Bank of America states in its 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) that increasing pressure to provide products and services on more attractive terms, including lower fees, lower cost investment strategies and higher interest rates on deposits, may impact its ability to effectively compete. Why it might matter: the bank states it may be disadvantaged by its size, the jurisdictions in which it operates, or more stringent regulatory requirements applicable to it than to nonbank competitors.

Bank of America states in its 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) that emerging technologies and the growth of e-commerce have made it easier for non-depository institutions to offer electronic securities trading with low or no fees and commissions, and that increased competition may reduce fee-based revenue through pricing pressure. Why it might matter: the bank notes the growth of and mergers among traditional financial services companies have also increased competition.

Schwab states in its 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) that increased price competition from other financial services firms to attract clients, such as reduced commissions, higher deposit rates, reduced mutual fund or ETF expense ratios, or the increased use of incentives, could impact its results. Why it might matter: Schwab states it continually monitors its pricing in relation to competitors and periodically adjusts fees and incentives to sustain its competitive position.

Edward Jones states in its 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) that it competes with major competitor brokerage firms that offer zero commissions for purchases and sales of stocks, ETFs and other brokerage products, and with firms offering lower cost, computer-based robo-advice. Why it might matter: Edward Jones notes clients can transfer their business to competing organizations at any time, and the firm also faces competition from fintech companies.

Morgan Stanley states in its 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) that it continues to experience price competition in its Institutional Securities business segment as the ability to execute trades electronically on automated platforms will likely continue the pressure on revenues. Why it might matter: the firm states the introduction of new technologies, including generative AI and tokenization, will likely continue the pressure on its revenues.

Deloitte (published May 20, 2026) states that competitive pressure may compress fees as planning outputs become easier to compare. Why it might matter: Deloitte also notes lower cost-to-serve can expand margins for firms that execute and maintain pricing.

McKinsey (published April 8, 2026) states fee pressure will be uneven, manifesting as demands for transparency and unbundled pricing rather than a blanket reduction in basis points. Why it might matter: McKinsey notes fee rates for relationships over $1 million have remained remarkably steady at about 104 basis points since 2019 even as digital tools have proliferated.

Survey data (published August 13, 2025) shows 48% of participants consider pricing and overall anticipated costs among the top three factors in choosing an advisor, indicating transparent, reasonable pricing is a dealmaker rather than simply being cheapest. Why it might matter: the source states transparent, reasonable pricing gives clients peace of mind and helps them budget.

Capgemini (published June 3, 2026) projects the robo advisory market will grow at a 44.1% CAGR for AUM between 2024 and 2030, and digital-first clients prefer robo-advisory platforms that deliver seamless, low-cost, self-directed experiences. Why it might matter: Capgemini notes specialized providers with differentiated value propositions are scaling faster, while mid-tier HNWIs increasingly rely on RIAs providing flexible, fiduciary advice.

Industry observers state that the platform tolls (data and support fees) appearing at large distributors are directly or indirectly traceable to the zeroing out of commissions in the brokerage industry, as revenue replacement must come from somewhere if loads are no longer charged on funds (trade report published September 29, 2026). Why it might matter: observers note distributors have real costs to distributing, though Merrill cannot lean as heavily on that argument for its full-service brokers.

The widespread adoption of data fees was predicted to offset declining transaction revenue, beginning in 2019 when Charles Schwab started charging for data it had historically provided for free (trade report published September 29, 2026). Why it might matter: the report notes Fidelity introduced ETF platform and revenue-sharing fees in March 2024, while UBS and Wells Fargo introduced data fees in the mid-2010s and 2020 respectively.

Schwab states in its 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) that the wealth management industry is highly competitive and characterized by aggressive price competition. Why it might matter: Edward Jones separately notes there has been ongoing fee compression across the mutual fund industry in recent years.

A consumer survey (published August 13, 2025) found nearly three-quarters (73%) of survey participants said transparency in fees and services is crucial for establishing an advisor's credibility, making fee transparency the top trust factor driving transparency. Why it might matter: the source identifies clear, upfront communication about costs as the most important factor for building trust.

Wealthtender's study (published August 13, 2025) reports pricing and overall anticipated cost is the top factor (48%) in final advisor selection, exerting competitive pressure on pricing. Why it might matter: the source cautions this does not mean choosing the cheapest option is best, and advises focusing on value for the fees paid.

A trade report (published October 26, 2026) states large team departures may now be structural given the attractive economics in RIA ownership, prompting Ameriprise to respond with reductions to platform fees, alongside cash retention bonuses, to retain advisors. Why it might matter: the report notes stronger recruiting and retention from the wirehouses has also slowed breakaways to independent broker-dealers.

The Wealthtender advisor search study (conducted July 2025, published August 13, 2025) found that fee transparency is a 73% priority for consumers researching financial advisors. Why it might matter: the study advises advisors to ensure their pricing is clearly communicated across all marketing materials.

Wealthtender (published August 13, 2025) reports consumers researching advisors prioritize fee transparency, professional credentials, and positive client reviews. Why it might matter: the source also advises consumers to focus on advisors who specialize in their particular needs and life stage.

According to Cerulli (published May 28, 2025), fee-based planning is the most preferred form of compensating an advisor among affluent investors, preferred by 36%, although some investors still prefer commission-based or no-fee services. Why it might matter: Cerulli notes this shift improves the standing of financial firms as fiduciaries since compensation is tied to portfolio performance rather than selling particular products.

Schwab states (2026 first-quarter earnings call, quarter ended March 31, 2026) that its model is informed by investors' preferences for lower explicit fees without sacrificing product access, convenience, or service. Why it might matter: Schwab states that if those preferences change in the future, it has flexibility to continue supporting investors and RIAs while still delivering strong returns.

According to McKinsey (published February 10, 2025), increasing demand for human advice is one of the factors behind stable to slightly increasing advisory fee rates across delivery models. Why it might matter: McKinsey notes that among investors with more than $1 million in investable assets, the share willing to pay a premium of 100 basis points or more grew by 50 percent.

McKinsey (published April 8, 2026) anticipates that fee pressure in wealth management will be uneven, manifesting as client demands for transparency and unbundled pricing rather than a blanket reduction in basis points. Why it might matter: McKinsey notes fee rates for relationships over $1 million have remained remarkably steady at about 104 basis points since 2019 even as digital tools proliferated.

Fidelity's 2025 Investor Insights Study (published October 9, 2025) finds that wealthy next-generation (Gen X, Y, and Z) high-net-worth households seek transparency in advisor compensation, along with broader life guidance and emerging investment products. Why it might matter: the study states advisors must adapt to these shifting dynamics to effectively serve this generation's distinctive demands.

Vanguard (published June 4, 2025) found that for digital advice, the key attributes valued by clients include the need for transparency (visibility of portfolio changes) and an awareness of fees. Why it might matter: Vanguard contrasts this with human advice, where value is mostly derived from a client's relationship with their financial advisor.

Schwab CEO Rick Wurster stated (2026 first-quarter earnings call, quarter ended March 31, 2026) that, according to research, more than half of the firm's clients are willing to pay for AI financial tools, which over time will create opportunities for new fee-based offers. Why it might matter: the CEO stated AI is already driving scale and efficiency by helping drive productivity across the firm.

The comparison of which firms lead or lag on fee structure changes and transparency cannot be validly made on this evidence as a whole, because the items are not on a same basis: they cover different fee types (data/shelf fees, trading commissions and margins, advisory fees), different scopes, and different time periods, with no shared metric against which firms are ranked. Within the narrower slice of data/shelf fees, trade-press reporting (published September 29, 2026) states Merrill Lynch is among the last major wealth management firms to maximize data/shelf fees, while Charles Schwab began charging for advisor data in 2019 earlier than peers, and Merrill notes its new data analytics fee scale is comparable to peers, with Wells Fargo levying up to $1.15 million, UBS between $150,000 and $300,000, and Morgan Stanley between $25,000 and $500,000; but these bear only on data/shelf fees, not on fee structure changes and transparency overall.
